subject: Banking
title: FinCEN Files: Banks Know
description: A 60-second lesson on FinCEN Files: Banks Know.

hook.text: The FinCEN Files showed banks filed 2 million suspicious activity reports but kept processing transactions.

buildup.text: US law requires banks to report suspicious transactions to FinCEN.

discovery.text: Banks treated SARs as paperwork, not action items. Filing the report was the end of their obligation.

twist.text: FinCEN receives 2 million reports annually with only 300 analysts to review them. The system is designed to fail.

climax.text: The FinCEN Files proved the anti-money-laundering system is theater. Banks report. No one investigates.

punchline.text: $2 trillion flagged. 2 million reports. 300 analysts. Compliance theater.

quiz.question: What happens after banks file suspicious activity reports?
options: Very little — FinCEN has only 300 analysts for 2 million annual reports

details.summary: The FinCEN Files leak in 2020 revealed that major global banks filed over 2,100 suspicious activity reports worth $2 trillion yet continued processing the flagged transactions, exposing a compliance system that monitors but rarely stops illicit money.
details.whyItMatters: The leak proved that banks often identify suspicious money flows but continue facilitating them. Filing a report satisfies legal requirements without actually preventing the crime.
takeaways: Banks filed suspicious activity reports covering $2 trillion in transactions
Major banks including HSBC, JPMorgan, and Deutsche Bank were named
Filing reports often fulfilled legal duties without stopping transactions

faq.question: Why do banks file reports but keep processing suspicious money?
faq.answer: Filing a Suspicious Activity Report satisfies the bank's legal obligation. Banks are not required to stop transactions based on suspicion alone. Freezing accounts without certainty could expose the bank to lawsuits from legitimate customers.

faq.question: Did any banks face consequences from the FinCEN Files?
faq.answer: Some banks faced increased regulatory scrutiny, but no major new penalties directly resulted from the leak. The revelations primarily exposed systemic weaknesses in the anti-money-laundering framework rather than specific bank violations.
